strengths: ReLIFT addresses a practical problem with a simple, interpretable mechanism: identify questions with zero successful rollouts and interleave supervised updates using teacher demonstrations.
The reported Qwen2.5-Math-7B results are promising: 51.1% average accuracy versus 45.5% for RL, 48.9% for SFT, and 49.7% for LUFFY.
Evaluation includes five mathematical benchmarks, MMLU-Pro, and three base models. Ablations examine demonstration selection and update scheduling.
Difficulty-stratified analyses and training curves provide useful observations about the complementary behavior of RL and SFT.
weaknesses: The central claim of overcoming fundamental RL capability limits is unsupported. Zero successes in eight samples does not establish that a question lies beyond a model’s capabilities. Figure 1 also shows RL improving on the initially hardest questions. These experiments support targeted teacher supervision, but do not distinguish acquiring new capabilities from increasing the probability of existing solutions. The statement that RL is inherently on-policy is also incorrect.

Evaluation details contain a major unresolved inconsistency: Appendix A.1 specifies an 8,192-token generation limit, while Tables 1–3 report many average response lengths exceeding this, including 26,583 for ReLIFT(all). If LEN uses another unit, that unit and its relationship to computational cost must be specified. As written, the evaluation protocol and central efficiency claims cannot be reconciled.

Important controls are missing, particularly SFT followed by RL using the same demonstration budget, and hybrid baselines matched for training tokens, compute, and teacher access. Standalone SFT uses a different learning rate and training duration. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate the benefit of adaptive interleaving from additional supervision or optimization choices; novelty over existing combinations of imitation and RL remains modest.

The claimed 13% demonstration requirement has unclear accounting. Figure 4 compares 8,320 demonstrations against 64,000 for SFT, whereas the described dataset contains 45,000 prompts and SFT runs for three epochs. Unique demonstrations, repeated exposures, and update counts are not distinguished. All experiments use precomputed demonstrations, so reduced online acquisition cost and end-to-end scalability are not demonstrated.

Several table entries require verification. ReLIFT(random) exactly repeats the RL baseline’s accuracy and length on all five mathematical benchmarks, despite additional supervised updates. The Qwen-7B base row likewise exactly repeats Qwen-Math-7B’s five mathematical accuracy/length pairs. These unexplained duplications weaken confidence in the ablation and extension results.

No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported. The gain over the closest hybrid baseline, LUFFY, is only 1.4 average points, and improvements over the strongest standalone baseline on the additional models are approximately one point. MMLU-Pro performance is essentially tied with LUFFY, limiting evidence for improved out-of-distribution generalization.

Reproducibility and contamination controls are incomplete. Buffer removal/reuse, duplicate handling, and optimizer-state management across RL/SFT updates are unspecified. Shuffling multiple-choice options does not prevent contamination from previously seen question content, and no explicit train–benchmark overlap audit is reported.

strengths: ReLIFT offers a simple, practically motivated approach: selectively interleave supervised updates on questions receiving zero rollout reward with ongoing RL training.
Table 1 reports encouraging performance: 51.1% average accuracy versus 45.5% for RL, 48.9% for SFT, and 49.7% for the reproduced LUFFY baseline.
The evaluation covers five mathematics benchmarks, MMLU-Pro, and three base models. Difficulty-specific analyses and scheduling/data-selection ablations provide useful initial evidence.
weaknesses: The central claim of overcoming fundamental RL capability limits is unsupported. Zero successes in eight samples does not establish that a question lies beyond the model’s capabilities; even a model with 20% success probability fails all eight trials about 17% of the time. Figure 1 also shows RL improving on the hardest group. The experiments establish benefits from teacher supervision, not a fundamental capability boundary.

The incremental contribution over existing combinations of imitation and RL is insufficiently isolated. Although LUFFY is reproduced, there is no conventional SFT-then-RL baseline using the same demonstration budget, nor an adequately controlled comparison of adaptive selection against a static hard-example curriculum. The headline +5.2-point comparison concerns a baseline without teacher demonstrations; the gain over LUFFY is only 1.4 points.

Important evaluation details are inconsistent or unexplained. Appendix A.1 specifies an 8,192-token generation limit, while tables report average response lengths above 26,000. If LEN measures characters instead, its units must be specified and the computational-efficiency interpretation justified. Table 2 also reproduces all five mathematics accuracy/length pairs from the RL baseline exactly for ReLIFT(random), requiring verification.

The 13% demonstration-efficiency claim has unclear accounting. Figure 4 reports 64,000 demonstrations for SFT, whereas training is described as three epochs over 45,000 prompts. Unique demonstrations, repeated exposures, and supervised token counts are not distinguished. All experiments use precomputed teacher solutions, and teacher-generation costs and end-to-end training costs are not measured.

There are no training-seed repetitions or uncertainty estimates. This matters for the 1.4-point gain over LUFFY, the 2-point scheduling-ablation difference, and roughly 1-point gains over the strongest RL/SFT baseline on the additional models. Repeated decoding on small benchmarks does not establish robustness to training randomness.

Comparisons confound training choices: standalone SFT uses a learning rate ten times higher than interleaved SFT and a different training duration, without a reported tuning study. Buffer removal/reuse, optimizer-state handling across objectives, and precise update accounting are also unspecified, limiting reproducibility.

Generalization and contamination claims exceed the evidence. ReLIFT essentially ties LUFFY on MMLU-Pro (52.5 versus 52.6), and shuffling answer options does not eliminate question-content contamination. No explicit training–benchmark overlap audit is reported. These unresolved methodological and reporting issues place the submission below the acceptance threshold despite promising results.

strengths: ReLIFT offers a simple, practical approach: use failed RL rollouts to select questions for interleaved supervised updates from a stronger teacher.
The reported main results are promising: 51.1 average accuracy versus 45.5 for RL, 48.9 for SFT, and 49.7 for LUFFY on six benchmarks.

The paper includes difficulty-stratified training analysis, scheduling and selection ablations, and experiments on three base models. These provide useful initial evidence for combining RL with targeted supervision.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol contains a major unresolved inconsistency. Appendix A.1 specifies an 8,192-token generation limit, but Tables 1–3 report average response lengths well above this, including 23,650 for ReLIFT(all). The length units and actual decoding limits must be clarified before the accuracy comparisons and nearly 10× efficiency claim can be trusted.

The central claim of overcoming fundamental RL capability limits is unsupported. Zero successes in eight samples does not establish that a question exceeds the model's capabilities; even a model with 20% success probability fails all eight attempts about 17% of the time. Figure 1 also shows RL improving on the hardest category. Larger sampling budgets and controlled capability analyses are needed.

The comparison does not establish the benefit over a conventional SFT-then-RL pipeline using the same selected demonstrations and comparable compute. Pure SFT uses a different learning rate and training budget. Against the closest hybrid baseline, LUFFY, the gain is only 1.4 points, with no training-seed variability or confidence intervals.

The demonstration-efficiency accounting is unclear. Figure 4 reports 64,000 demonstrations for SFT, whereas training is described as three epochs over 45,000 prompts. Unique demonstrations, repeated training exposures, and teacher-generation costs are not distinguished. All experiments use precomputed demonstrations, so online acquisition and its claimed scalability remain untested.

The key selection ablation needs verification: ReLIFT(random) exactly reproduces the RL baseline's accuracies and lengths on all five mathematics benchmarks, while its MMLU-Pro response length changes dramatically. Buffer removal, reuse, and deduplication rules are also unspecified, making the adaptive schedule difficult to reproduce.

Claims of consistently substantial gains and concise responses do not generalize across models. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, ReLIFT improves average accuracy by only 1.0 point over RL while increasing average response length from 913 to 4,421. On Qwen2.5-7B, its advantage over SFT is only 1.1 points.

Benchmark contamination controls are insufficiently documented: shuffling MMLU-Pro answer options does not remove question-level contamination, and training–test overlap checks for the mathematics datasets are not reported. Together with the reporting inconsistencies and missing controlled comparisons, this leaves the evidence below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: ReLIFT offers a simple, practical strategy: use failed RL rollouts to select questions for intermittent supervised updates from verified teacher demonstrations.

The evaluation includes six benchmarks, four base models, and relevant hybrid baselines, including LUFFY and demonstration-count-matched SFT followed by RL. On Qwen2.5-Math-7B, ReLIFT achieves 52.6% average accuracy versus 50.9% for the strongest reproduced hybrid baselines.

The scheduling and selection ablations provide useful evidence for adaptive training on difficult questions. Reported student-training costs and demonstration usage are lower than those of the main hybrid baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning capabilities that RL cannot acquire is not established. Zero successes in eight samples does not demonstrate that a question lies outside the model’s capabilities; even a model with 20% success probability fails all eight samples about 17% of the time. The study lacks high-budget sampling or controlled skill-acquisition experiments, and the initial RL/SFT comparison also uses substantially different learning rates and training objectives.

The contribution is not cleanly separated from entropy regularization. Figure 5 places ReLIFT without this term at approximately 49.8%, below LUFFY and SFT-then-RL at 50.9%. Thus, the regularizer’s contribution exceeds the reported advantage over these baselines. Comparable regularization and tuning for the baselines are needed to attribute the gain to targeted interleaving.

The strongest matched-baseline improvement is 1.7 percentage points, but no training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported. Averaging 32 generations on small benchmarks reduces sampling noise without establishing training robustness. Hybrid comparisons are also absent for the additional base models, limiting evidence that the advantage generalizes.

The online acquisition and efficiency claims exceed the demonstrated setting. Appendix B states that demonstrations were collected beforehand, and the entire training pool was filtered using teacher correctness and response length. The reported 8,640 demonstrations therefore measure selected supervision rather than the full teacher-data acquisition requirement. Teacher generation and verification costs are excluded, and ReLIFT takes more student GPU time than standalone RL or SFT.

Important implementation and ablation details remain unclear: buffer removal or reuse, duplicate handling, optimizer-state sharing between RL and SFT, and the precise data-selection policy for uniform scheduling. The main GRPO equation uses standard-deviation normalization, whereas Appendix B says this is removed. The collapse of ReLIFT(all) also changes supervision volume and frequency simultaneously, so it does not isolate the scheduling mechanism.

Several claims overstate the tables. ReLIFT is not consistently best or second-best on every benchmark, and its additional-model results do not uniformly surpass both SFT and RL. OOD evidence is limited to MMLU-Pro, where it trails RL for Qwen2.5-7B. Shuffling answer options does not establish absence of contamination, and no explicit training–evaluation overlap audit is described.

strengths: ReLIFT is a simple, practical approach: use failed RL rollouts to select teacher demonstrations and interleave targeted supervised updates with RL.

The main experiments include relevant hybrid baselines, including LUFFY and demonstration-budget-matched SFT followed by RL. ReLIFT reports the highest average accuracy: 52.6 versus 50.9 for both strongest hybrid baselines.

Evaluation covers six benchmarks and four base models. Scheduling, example-selection, and entropy ablations provide useful evidence, and the reported training costs are lower than those of the evaluated hybrid baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim about learning capabilities beyond the base model is not established. Zero successes among eight samples does not demonstrate inability: a question with a true 10% success probability will produce eight failures about 43% of the time. The 120-step comparison also uses substantially different SFT and RL learning rates and does not establish matched computational budgets. These experiments support a practical difficulty heuristic, not the stronger conclusion that SFT learns what RL cannot.

The contribution is an incremental combination of difficulty filtering, teacher supervision, and alternating optimization. Its empirical attribution remains unresolved: Figure 5 places ReLIFT without entropy regularization at approximately 49.8, below the 50.9 hybrid baselines. Comparisons that give those baselines comparable entropy regularization and tuning are needed to isolate the proposed scheduling and selection mechanism.

The headline improvement of 6.7 points is against a previous RLVR baseline; the gain over the strongest reproduced hybrid methods is only 1.7 points. No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported. Repeating inference 32 times on small benchmarks reduces sampling noise but does not establish robustness across training runs or test questions. Additional-model experiments omit the strongest hybrid baselines.

The online acquisition and efficiency claims exceed the experiments. Appendix B states that demonstrations were collected beforehand, and the training pool itself is filtered using teacher correctness and response length. Consequently, using 8,640 demonstrations during updates does not establish the end-to-end cost of acquiring only those demonstrations online. Teacher generation and verification costs are not included. ReLIFT also costs more than standalone RL or SFT and generates longer responses than RL.

Table 1 contains a material reporting anomaly: SFT and RL with SFT loss have identical accuracies on five benchmarks and identical response lengths on all six, despite different training procedures. The RL-with-SFT-loss overall length also does not match its listed lengths. These results require clarification. Separately, the claim that ReLIFT ranks first or second on every benchmark is contradicted by the table, including AIME-2025 and MATH-500.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The buffer description does not specify whether consumed examples are removed, how repeated questions are handled, or whether optimizer states are shared across RL and supervised updates. Appendix B changes the advantage normalization shown in Equation 1, leaving the implemented objective insufficiently explicit. These details affect both the adaptive schedule and the demonstration budget.

Generalization and contamination claims need stronger support. MMLU-Pro is the only OOD benchmark, and ReLIFT underperforms RL there for Qwen2.5-7B. Shuffling answer options does not eliminate question-level contamination, and no explicit train–test overlap audit is reported. The evidence supports promising benchmark improvements, but not the paper's broad claims of superior generalization and new reasoning capabilities.

strengths: ReLIFT offers a simple, practical approach: use failed RL rollouts to identify questions needing teacher demonstrations, then interleave targeted supervised updates with RL.

The main model achieves 52.6% average accuracy versus 50.9% for LUFFY and demonstration-matched SFT-then-RL, with shorter average responses and lower reported training costs than these hybrid baselines.
Experiments cover six benchmarks and four base models. ReLIFT consistently improves aggregate accuracy over the reproduced standalone SFT and RL baselines.
The selection and scheduling ablations provide useful evidence: accuracy falls from 52.6% to 49.1% with uniform scheduling and to 45.5% when demonstrations target non-hardest questions.
weaknesses: The central claim about learning capabilities that RL cannot acquire is not established. Zero successes in eight samples does not demonstrate that a question lies beyond the model's capabilities; even a model with 20% success probability fails all eight attempts about 17% of the time. The short training-dynamics study supports relative effectiveness under specific settings, rather than an inherent limitation of RL.

Important comparisons remain confounded. Standalone SFT uses a learning rate 50 times the interleaved SFT rate, and the motivation experiment matches steps rather than training exposure or compute. There is no demonstration-matched hybrid baseline on the additional models or comparison against RL explicitly tuned to maintain exploration. These omissions limit attribution of gains to the proposed selection and scheduling mechanism.

The gain over the strongest hybrid baselines is 1.7 percentage points, but no training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported. Sampling 32 responses per question improves evaluation precision but does not address training variability or the small number of independent AIME problems.

The online acquisition and efficiency claims exceed the experiments. All demonstrations are collected beforehand, and the training pool itself is filtered using teacher correctness and response length. Teacher-generation costs and online latency are not included. ReLIFT also requires more GPU time and longer responses than standalone RL, so efficiency advantages should be explicitly restricted to particular hybrid comparisons.

Several reported results require correction or clarification. The SFT and RL-with-SFT-loss rows repeat every per-benchmark response length and five of six accuracy values, while reporting different overall lengths. The claim of best or second-best performance on every benchmark is contradicted by Table 1, including AIME-24 and AIME-25.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: buffer removal or reuse, optimizer-state handling across update types, and the exact uniform-schedule ablation are insufficiently specified. Equation 1 includes normalization that Appendix B says is removed in the experiments.

The contribution is an incremental refinement of combining teacher supervision with RL, and the broader generalization claims need qualification. Only one OOD benchmark is tested; ReLIFT underperforms RL on MMLU-Pro for Qwen2.5-7B, and its Llama aggregate remains below the instruction-tuned reference. Overall, the promising empirical results do not yet fully resolve the comparison and evidential weaknesses needed for acceptance.
